title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hook: a boy who had never seen another person, and the rain that followed him

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice begins, and your line, admitting what he lacks. A king with everything but a son asked his counselors, and Sumantra remembered a prophecy.

Deep in a forest lives a sage, Vibhandaka, and his son, Rishyashringa. The boy has grown up with only his father, the trees, the sacred fire and the animals. He has never been to a town, never seen anyone but his father. Meanwhile, in the kingdom of Anga, a long way off, the rain has stopped. Fields crack. Wells sink. The king, Romapada, asks his priests what to do, and they give him an odd answer: bring the forest boy here, and the rain will come with him.
screen: `A BOY WHO'S ONLY SEEN HIS FATHER.` → `A KINGDOM WITHOUT RAIN.` → `BRING THE FOREST BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sumantra tells it. The king's people can't just march in and take a sage's son. So they send young women from the city into the forest, with sweets and garlands. Rishyashringa, who has never met anyone, thinks they're young hermits from another ashram, and welcomes them with water and fruit, as a host should. They give him sweets he takes for a new kind of fruit, and invite him to their hermitage. He goes with them, all the way to Anga, and the moment he enters the kingdom, the rain pours down. The king honors him and gives him his daughter, Shanta, in marriage. That's the story Sumantra brings to Dasharatha, who goes himself to Anga, to his old friend Romapada, and brings Rishyashringa and Shanta home to Ayodhya with great honor. Then the sacrifice. On the bank of the Sarayu, the horse is released to wander for a year, followed by guards, and when it returns the great rite is performed: altars of brick, priests from far kingdoms, gifts given away on an enormous scale. Why the rain story? It tells us who Rishyashringa is: so untouched, so simple and so full of tapas that the sky answers wherever he goes. And in this telling, nobody seizes him. He is invited, and he comes.
screen: `THE KINGDOM OF ANGA, WITHOUT RAIN.` · `THE FOREST BOY IS INVITED OUT.` · `WHERE HE GOES, RAIN FOLLOWS.` · `THE HORSE IS RELEASED FOR A YEAR.` · then, large: `RISHYASHRINGA.`

segments.voice: Rishyashringa met strangers the way a host meets guests, with water, fruit and an open door. Let each breath arrive like a guest, without pulling it in, and see each one off kindly. Nothing to make happen; just keep the door open.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. To perform it, the king brings Rishyashringa, the forest sage whose coming brought rain to a dry kingdom, to Ayodhya.
Your line: where he goes, rain follows. A dry kingdom, and one simple guest. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rishyashringa is honored at some local temples in India, and his story is told as part of the Ramayana's opening, as the reason the rain-bringing sage leads Dasharatha's rites.

fork.setup: you're the king of Anga. a holy boy in the forest can end your drought, but his father would never let him go. what do you do?
options: send people to befriend him and invite him.
wait for the rain on your own.
fork.reveal: he sends visitors with gifts who invite the boy out. Rishyashringa comes, the rain falls, and he marries the king's daughter.

original.note: Sanskrit ṛśyaśṛṅga: deer-horned, from ṛśya, a kind of antelope, and śṛṅga, horn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story before the real one starts.
what it means: it shows who the sage is, someone the sky answers, and why he must be invited, not taken.

what a scholar hears: the Rishyashringa episode is also told in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva; in Valmiki's southern recension Shanta is Romapada's daughter, while some later tellings make her Dasharatha's daughter adopted by Romapada.
guess: the horse rite, for which the king brings a rain-bringing sage
a rain rite Romapada holds to end the long drought in Anga
a wedding feast for Shanta and the forest sage in Ayodhya

chat.says: How did a boy from the deep forest end up in a faraway kingdom?
options: He was invited. He welcomed the visitors as a host, went with them, and rain followed.
The king's soldiers seized him in the night and carried him off to Anga.
His father Vibhandaka sent him to Anga to marry the princess there.
chat.meaning: In Sumantra's telling, nobody seizes Rishyashringa. Visitors invite him, he goes with them to Anga, and the rain pours down.

Rishyashringa.meaning: the forest sage whose coming brings rain

Anga.meaning: a kingdom struck by drought, ruled by Romapada

Shanta.meaning: the princess given to Rishyashringa in marriage

tapas.meaning: the heat of discipline and austerity

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 9–11 (Rishyashringa, Anga, Shanta)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 12–14 (the horse sacrifice on the Sarayu)

notes: Shanta's parentage differs between recensions and later tellings; stated with that caveat in the trapdoor. Confirm.
The women sent into the forest are courtesans in the text; the script says 'young women from the city'. Keeper may prefer the text's word.
howItsDone mentions local temple traditions honoring Rishyashringa without naming one (e.g. Kigga near Sringeri); a Keeper may want to name one.
